headline: Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra prototype with Nvidia N1X chip found by reviewer, showing promise but also 'warts'
summary: A reviewer 'accidentally' discovered a Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra prototype featuring Nvidia's N1X SoC. Early tests reveal promising GPU performance but highlight significant driver and power management issues.
details: A TechPowerUp reader 'accidentally' stumbled upon a Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra prototype, which houses an Nvidia RTX Spark N1X SoC. This pre-release hardware offers a glimpse into the next generation of 'AI laptops'.

The N1X chip is designed with large pools of unified memory and competent GPUs for non-datacenter AI work. It features 10 MediaTek-designed ARM CPU cores (5p5e configuration, 20 threads total) and a GPU purportedly equivalent to a desktop RTX 4070 or mobile RTX 5070.

The prototype can support up to 128 GB of LPDDR5X unified memory, though the tested machine only had 24 GB. Initial Phoronix AI test suite results were mixed, with few tests reliably working, likely due to pre-production drivers.

The system and its drivers appear buggy and unoptimized, particularly regarding power management. The tester found erratic TDP behavior and power plans, with older drivers from November 2025 and preview drivers failing to produce CUDA test results.

Head-to-head benchmarks are challenging due to the N1X's 24 GB VRAM compared to limited VRAM on desktop RTX cards. There's a strong possibility that final hardware will perform better, as this pre-production unit had numerous issues including with the LCD and idle current draw.
In CPU benchmarks, Cinebench 2024 multi-threaded test scored 1386 points, trailing the 12-core Macbook M4 Pro. Cinebench 2026 yielded 5771, falling behind the Apple M4 Max.

GPU tests showed varied results; 3DMark Port Royal achieved 26-31 FPS with older drivers, while Nomad got 20-21 FPS. Unigine Superposition, however, improved with the 616.00 software, reaching 56-58 FPS.

Gaming performance was sluggish, with multiple-second stutters and erratic GPU clock speeds. Games like Helldivers 2 crashed the system, and GPGPU integer tests also failed, possibly due to ARM emulation layer issues or specific N1X implementation problems.

Despite the performance issues, the reviewer praised the machine's high build quality, keyboard feel, touchpad input, and display. While technically serviceable, opening the device revealed many snap-on aluminum panels making actual repairs difficult.
